pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words, with the exercise's own numbers cited where a question asks for evidence; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Walk me through how your `Decode` gets from `dst any` to writing a string into a struct field. Why does it need a pointer, and what does it do if it doesn't get one?
expected_points: an interface value is a (type, value) pair; reflect.ValueOf/TypeOf open that pair
reflect.ValueOf(dst) holds a copy unless dst is a pointer; Elem() dereferences it to something addressable, and only addressable values are settable
iterate Type().NumField(), read Tag via StructField.Tag.Lookup, switch on Value.Kind(), call SetString/SetBool/SetInt
unexported fields can be read but not set — skip them with IsExported
a non-pointer, nil, or pointer-to-non-struct target returns ErrNotStructPointer; a library validates instead of letting reflect panic at its caller

questions.prompt: Quote your own benchmark numbers for the two decoders. The reflect one is several times slower with the same (zero) allocations — explain where its time goes, then give me two costs of reflection that have nothing to do with speed.
expected_points: runtime kind switches, per-call tag parsing, indexed field lookups, and nothing inlines or specializes — the compiler cannot see through reflect.Value
reflection does not inherently allocate; it allocates when you box (Interface(), reflect.New, any) — the folk belief 'reflection = allocations' is wrong here and they have the number to prove it
compile-time safety is lost: struct tags are unchecked strings, so a typo or a renamed field fails at runtime, only for inputs that exercise it
tooling blindness: rename/find-usages don't follow tags, dead-code elimination can't prove reflected fields unused
readability and debuggability: reflect stack traces and code are opaque to the next reader

questions.prompt: Name two places where reflection is the right answer and two where it isn't, and give me the rule you used to sort them.
expected_points: justified where types are genuinely unknown until runtime and the boundary is real: encoding/json, database/sql Scan, fmt, text/template — decoding into types the library author cannot see
justified in test/tool code (DeepEqual, diffing, fixtures) and in once-at-startup work, where cost is amortized to nothing
not justified in a hot path of your own service where the set of types is known and finite
not justified as a substitute for generics when the caller knows the type
the rule: how many types are there really, when must the decision be made, and who pays for a mistake

questions.prompt: What guarantee does `UnsafeString(b)` break, what must its caller promise, and why is `uintptr` a worse thing to hold than `unsafe.Pointer`?
expected_points: it returns a string aliasing b's array — Go's guarantee that strings are immutable is now the caller's responsibility
the caller must never modify b while the string is reachable, and must not let the string outlive that guarantee; violations are silent wrong answers (map hashing, cached keys), not crashes

unsafe.Pointer is a pointer the GC understands: it keeps the object alive, and — for the one case where Go does relocate memory, a goroutine stack that grows — the runtime rewrites it. Heap objects never move. A uintptr gets neither treatment.
pointer arithmetic must therefore stay inside a single expression; unsafe is outside the Go 1 compatibility promise; go vet's unsafeptr and the race detector's checkptr are the available checks
UnsafeBytes is worse still: string data may be read-only or shared, so writing through it can fault or corrupt

questions.prompt: Your generator uses reflection to write code that avoids reflection. Explain why that isn't a contradiction, what `//go:generate` actually does, and what the generated file bought you besides speed.
expected_points: reflection at generate time runs once on a developer's machine; the cost that matters is per-request, not per-release
//go:generate is only a comment: go build/test ignore it, `go generate ./...` is a separate human- or CI-run step with no caching or ordering
the output is committed, so a clone builds with no generator, no protoc, no network — as with the gRPC lesson's .pb.go files
unsupported types are rejected at generate time for every field, instead of at runtime only when someone sets that key
generated code is ordinary Go: inlinable, profilable under its own name, readable in review; the header `// Code generated ... DO NOT EDIT.` is the convention tools rely on
costs: an extra build step, generated files in diffs, drift unless CI regenerates and diffs, and a generator to maintain

questions.prompt: Sort these three: a `Max[T cmp.Ordered]` helper, a library decoding arbitrary JSON into user structs, and adding `String()` to 30 enum constants. Generics, reflection, or codegen — and what changes your answer?
expected_points: Max is generics: the caller knows the type, the compiler can specialize, zero runtime cost
the JSON library is reflection: user types are unknowable at library build time and there is no build step you can impose on your users
the enum String() methods are codegen (stringer): finite, mechanical, drift-prone by hand, and free at runtime
what changes it: whether the type set is finite and known, whether you control the build, how hot the path is, and how a mistake surfaces

questions.prompt: A colleague adds `UnsafeString` in three places to 'avoid copies': a map lookup `m[string(b)]`, a comparison `string(b) == key`, and scanning a 16 KiB request body. What do you say in review?
expected_points: the map lookup and the comparison already allocate nothing — the compiler special-cases them, so the unsafe versions add risk for zero gain
short conversions that don't escape land in a stack buffer anyway
the large read-only scan is the case that can genuinely pay — their Lookup benchmark showed the same allocation count but 16 KiB vs 64 B
even then it needs a benchmark, a comment stating the aliasing invariant, and confidence nothing retains the string
